Our 51-year-old female patient was presented for the first time
to physiatrists in 2006 and diagnosed with axial-spondyloarthropathy (SpA) HLA-B27 positive.
SPS was diagnosed 7 years after initial symptoms. SPS should be taken into consideration
in HLA-B27 positive patients if stiffness of paravertebral and abdominal muscles progresses
during SpA therapy.

A 51-year-old woman presented for the first time to the physiatrist in the Department of Physical Medicine, Rehabilitation and
Rheumatology of University Hospital Centre Split, in November
of 2006. She was suffering severe pain in the lumbar region and
moderate pain in the cervical region of the spine. During physical
examination her cervical and lumbar paravertebral muscles were
painful and rigid. The limitations of the movements in the lumbar
and cervical regions were noted. Plain radiographs of the cervical
and lumbar spine, as well as computed tomography of the lumbar
spine showed mild degenerative changes. The patient received
ibuprofen (1200–1600 mg/day), during 1-month period.
At that time, she was prescribed periodical intensive physical
therapy that included exercises of stretching and relaxation of the
spine muscles, mobilization of the lumbar and cervical spine, thermotherapy and hydrotherapy until April 2008. Performed physical therapy showed some success. The patient still presented an
inflammatory back pain in the lumbar spine including morning
stiffness lasting up to 2 hours that tended to improve after exercise
and frequent nocturnal awakenings.
Anamnesis revealed that patient’s initial symptoms began in
her 40s and included pain and morning stiffness of the cervical
and lumbar spine and unilateral heel pain. Her father had ankylosing spondylitis (AS), HLA-B27 positive. No clinical evidence or
anamnestic data of psoriatic changes of the skin, genitourinary,
gastrointestinal, and ocular infections were obtained. Physical
examination of patient revealed loss of cervical and lumbar lordosis and pain and rigidity of cervical and lumbar paravertebral
muscles. The range of spinal movements was reduced: modified
Schober’s test 2 cm, chest expansion 1. 5 cm, lumbar lateral bending 67 cm (distance between the tip of the third finger and the
floor). Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) was calculated to be 5. 3 and Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis
Functional Index (BASFI) scores was 8. 7. In laboratory findings

A laboratory measurement of the anti-GAD antibody in serum was
167 U/mL (normal range 0–0. 9 U/mL). EMG showed a continuous
motor unit activity of both agonist and antagonist muscles at the
same time. Patient fulfilled Dalakas criteria for the diagnoses of
typical SPS [6].

hemogram, routine biochemical analysis, acute phase reactants,
and tumor markers were all within normal range. The results of
the immunological tests including antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anticyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, C3 and C4
complement protein, antithyreoglobulin antibodies were negative.
The results of urine culture, stool culture, urogenital swab, and
serology of hepatitis were negative. HLA typization showed A1/3,
B27/44; Bw4, and Cw2 genotype. Radiography of the sacroiliac
(SI) joints showed sings of bilateral sacroiliitis, while magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) of the SI joints did not confirm the previous findings. MRI studies of the lumbar, thoracic, and cervical
spine excluded myelopathy and typical radiographic features of
SpA. Scintigraphy of the skeleton with technecium-99 m diphosponate showed accumulation of signal in the corpuses of second,
third, fourth, and fifth lumbar vertebrae. Radiologist from the University Hospital Center Zagreb was consulted and concluded that
this was the case of advanced osteoarthritis of SI joints, without
signs of inflammatory axial disease.
However, we concluded that this was the case of axial SpA
because the patient fulfilled the European Spondyloarthritides
Study Group (ESSG) and AMOR SpA classification criteria for
SpA.
The patient was prescribed indomethacin (150 mg/day) for
2 months that rapidly reduced the pain, but it did not help with the
stiffness. A partial relief of stiffness and rigidity occurred during
physical therapy and consumption of diazepam (4–6 mg/day).
In the second half of the 2008, patient’s clinical condition
worsened and a constant spasm of paravertebral muscles occurred.
Spasms were accompanied by rigidity of abdominal muscles causing detectable inclination of the spine. Patient, who already had
limitations in the everyday activities, started to feel imbalance
due to change of the posture. This resulted with three falls, two
of which ended up with nasal bones’ fractures. After the patient
complained on everyday chest pain with deep breathing, the internal medicine specialist was consulted and excluded rare but severe
cardiopulmonary manifestations of SpA. Other rheumatologists
were consulted and they confirmed the working diagnosis.
From December 2008 to December 2009, the patient was
treated with sulfasalazine (2000–3000 mg/day) but this therapy
was ceased because of ineffectiveness. In March 2010 patient
repeated MRI of SI joints, lumbar, thoracic, and cervical spine and
no progression of degenerative changes, nor new signs of inflammatory disease could be seen. The patient’s condition in the year
2010 was complicated by occasional spasms in the muscles of both
legs. The neurologist made comprehensive neurological examination and excluded pyramidal and extrapyramidal disorders.
In the beginning of 2011 a biological therapy for SpA was
taken into consideration. Interferon Gamma Release Assays for
the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis infection and Cyfra 21-1 tumor
marker were positive. A blood glucose level was elevated. Extensive pulmonary examination revealed no pathological substrate.
Repeated testing of Cyfra 21-1 was performed and Cyfra 21-1 was
in the normal range. Endocrinologist detected IDDM and excluded
other endocrinology and metabolic diseases. These findings and
patient’s discomfort were the reason why she was not included in
biological therapy.
At that time the patient was taking meloksikam (15 mg/day)

and attended physical therapy periodically. However, the rigidity
of whole spine, especially lumbar segment and abdominal muscles, as well as reduction in movements of cervical spine were still
present. Due to limitation in everyday functioning the patient still
needed constant help to perform everyday activities.
In the beginning of 2013 a rheumatologist at a Department of
Physical Medicine, Rehabilitation and Rheumatology of University Hospital Centre Split suspected that this was the case of SPS.
